model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe the place where I go when I want to think. It is a canal, behind an old mill building, and it is about fifteen minutes from my house on foot.

So I found it by accident. There was road works on my normal street, so I go a different way, and I see this path next to the water. Before that I don't know it is there, even I live here six years.

Usually I walk maybe twenty minutes and then I sit down. There is a gate on the water, I don't know the English word for this, and I sit on it. Sometimes I take a coffee with me. There is no signal for my phone in this place, so nobody can call me.

It helps me to think because it is very quiet there. In my flat it is not quiet, my neighbours are noisy and there is always something. But there it is only the water and some birds. So my head is more clear and I can think about my problem. It is a very nice place and I feel very relaxed. So this is the quiet place where I go to think.

what_caps_it.point: Almost every sentence opens with 'so' or 'and', so the turn lists instead of building.
The story of finding it starts in the past and finishes in the present.
'Quiet', 'noisy', 'nice', 'relaxed' carry the entire description between them.

model_answers.label: The target — same place, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'll talk about a stretch of canal towpath about fifteen minutes' walk from my flat, tucked away behind an old mill that hasn't been used for years.

I came across it completely by accident. There were roadworks on the route I normally take, so I ended up cutting through an industrial estate and coming out onto the water. I remember thinking it was odd that I'd lived here for six years and never known it was there. That was two summers ago, and I've been going most weeks ever since.

What I do is fairly unvarying. I walk for about twenty minutes, as far as a set of lock gates, and then I sit on the beam of the gate with my feet over the water. Sometimes I take a coffee, though half the time I forget. The important thing, I think, is that there's no phone signal down there at all, so the decision about whether to look at my phone gets taken away from me.

As for why it helps — it isn't really the quiet on its own, because it isn't silent. There's water moving through the gates the whole time and a low hum from the ring road. It's more that nothing there is waiting for me. At home there's always something in my line of sight that needs doing, whereas on the towpath the only thing in front of me is water. I find I do the actual thinking on the walk back rather than while I'm sitting there, which suggests it's the walking that does half the work. Either way, it's the only twenty minutes in my week when nobody can reach me.

what_lifts_it.point: A past perfect and a present perfect replace the band 6's run of flat past simples.
'Tucked away', 'came across', 'in my line of sight' — chunks doing the descriptive work.
'What I do is' and 'as for why' shape the turn; nothing is joined with a bare 'so'.

annotations.span: I'd lived here for six years and never known it was there

annotations.why: One backshift per story is enough to show two layers of time.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The place is a stretch of canal towpath behind a derelict mill, about a quarter of an hour on foot from where I live, and I stumbled on it entirely by chance.

There were roadworks on my usual route, so I cut through an industrial estate and came out on the water, and I can remember standing there faintly annoyed with myself — six years in the same postcode and I'd never once gone two streets further. Not that it's picturesque, particularly. It's a working waterway with rubbish in the reeds.

What I do there barely varies. Twenty minutes on foot to a set of lock gates, then I sit on the beam with my feet hanging over the water for as long as I can be bothered. There's no signal down there, which means the question of whether to check my phone simply never comes up, and that turns out to matter far more than the quiet does.

Because it isn't quiet, in fairness. Water comes through the gates the whole time and there's a drone from the ring road behind the trees. What it is, is undemanding — nothing on that towpath is waiting for me to deal with it, whereas at home there's never a sightline without a job in it. And I've noticed the thinking tends to happen on the walk back rather than on the gate itself, which makes me suspect that what I actually go for isn't the place at all. It's the twenty minutes of being unreachable.

what_lifts_it.point: A cleft — 'What it is, is undemanding' — where band 7 used a plain adjective clause.
'Derelict', 'stumbled on', 'undemanding' are chosen for shade of meaning, not rarity.
It argues against its own description twice and still lands on one idea.

annotations.span: I stumbled on it entirely by chance

annotations.why: 'Stumbled on' carries 'found' and 'by accident' in a single word.

annotations.span: Not that it's picturesque, particularly.
annotations.label: Concedes against its own praise
annotations.why: Undercut yourself once and everything else you claim sounds earned.

annotations.span: there's never a sightline without a job in it

annotations.why: A single original picture beats five borrowed idioms.

I would like to describe a park which I use. It is near my house, about ten minutes if I walk, and I pass a church to arrive there.

It is not a big park. There is a football field, and there is a path around it, and there is some trees on one side. Also there is a small playground for the children.

model_answers.label: The target — same park, better language
model_answers.transcript:
It's a recreation ground about ten minutes from my front door, past the church and over a footbridge. Officially it has a name, but nobody uses it — everyone just calls it the rec.

It isn't much to look at. There's a football pitch that floods every winter, a tarmac path round the outside, and a line of lime trees along the road that take most of the traffic noise out. The far corner is completely overgrown, which I think is deliberate, because nobody has touched it in the four years I've been going.

I go three mornings a week, always before seven, and I do three laps of the path, which comes to about two miles. Then on Sundays I take my niece, and that's a different sort of visit altogether — my niece is at the age where the swings are the entire point of the outing, so we're there for an hour and I never make it round the path once.

As for what I'd miss if they built on it — it wouldn't really be the running, because I could run along the canal instead. It would be the fact that I see the same people every week without ever having arranged anything. There's a man with two greyhounds, a couple who always argue quietly by the gate, half a dozen people I only ever nod at. You can't get that indoors, and you certainly can't get it by planning it. That's what a scruffy field does that a nicer, further-away park couldn't.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The place I use is a recreation ground ten minutes' walk away, over a footbridge and past a church. It has an official name on the sign, which I have never once heard anybody say out loud.

It's a fairly unpromising piece of land — a pitch that turns to mud by November, a tarmac loop round the edge, and a row of limes doing a surprising amount of work against the traffic. One corner has been left to go wild, and rather to my surprise the council seem to have done that on purpose. Whether by design or by neglect, it's the only patch with any birds in it.

My own use of it is dull and regular: three laps before seven, three mornings a week. Sundays are a different proposition, because I have my niece with me, and at four years old the swings are non-negotiable, so the running never happens at all. I've stopped pretending otherwise and started taking a flask.

What I'd miss, though, isn't the exercise. I could run somewhere else easily enough. It's that the place produces a kind of company nobody has to organise — the man with the greyhounds, the couple who bicker by the gate, the handful of people I've nodded at for years without ever learning a name. Were it built on, that would simply stop, and it isn't the sort of thing you can reopen somewhere more convenient. Scruffy and close beats handsome and twenty minutes away, every time.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Were it built on' — inversion replaces the band 7's standard second conditional.
'Unpromising', 'non-negotiable', 'bicker' are picked for shade rather than for size.
The close is an aphorism about places, not a summary of this place.

annotations.why: Same conditional, higher register, and it still sounds spoken.

annotations.label: A formal word used playfully
annotations.why: Borrowing a work word for family life is a very natural move.

annotations.span: the place produces a kind of company nobody has to organise
annotations.label: Abstracts the benefit in one phrase

annotations.span: Scruffy and close beats handsome and twenty minutes away, every time.
annotations.label: Closes on a general principle
annotations.why: End one rung above the story and the whole turn sounds considered.

annotations.why: Do not pause inside the phrase; keep it as a single group.

It's long and narrow, with units down one side and a table under the window at the far end. A galley kitchen, I think you'd call it. It would have to be the kitchen, which is at the back of the flat and, objectively, the least attractive room in it. I've never once shown it to a visitor on purpose, and yet that is where they all end up.

It's a galley — units along one wall, a table at the far end under a window that looks onto a yard containing three bins and a fig tree which has stubbornly refused to fruit. The place I'd choose is the covered market in the middle of town, which is an iron and glass hall from the 1880s with about forty stalls in it.

It's busy most days, but Saturday between about ten and one is when it becomes genuinely unpleasant. There's only one main aisle running the length of the building, so the whole thing behaves like a bottleneck — if two people stop to talk in the middle, everything behind them comes to a standstill. And they do stop, constantly, because half the town is in there at once. Nobody plans for that.

The reason so many go is partly price, since the fruit and veg is a fraction of what the supermarket charges, and partly loyalty, because the stalls have been run by the same families for years. My mother still refuses to buy fish anywhere else. She's been buying from the same man since before I was born, and she isn't alone in that.

How I feel about it depends entirely on what I'm there for. If I need something specific, I find it genuinely stressful — you can't move, you can't hear what anybody is saying, and it takes forty minutes to do fifteen minutes of shopping. But if I've got no particular plan, it's the only place in town where I run into people I haven't seen for months, and that only happens because it's crowded. So I've more or less stopped resenting it. I just go early when I'm in a hurry.

I'd pick the covered market in town — a Victorian hall with an iron roof, forty-odd stalls, and a single aisle running the entire length of it. It has looked more or less the same since the 1880s.

That one aisle is the whole problem. On a Saturday morning, roughly ten till one, the place is heaving, and since there's nowhere to step aside, two people greeting each other in the middle will bring the building to a halt. Which they do, endlessly, because half the town is in there at the same time.

What draws everybody is partly cost, as the fruit and veg goes for a fraction of supermarket prices, and partly loyalty, because most of the stalls have been in the same families for two or three generations and buying elsewhere feels faintly disloyal. My mother has used the same fishmonger for thirty years and would not dream of changing.

As for how I feel about it, that depends on what I've come for. Needing something specific, I find it close to unbearable — you shuffle, you can't hear, and a fifteen-minute errand swallows an hour. Go in with nothing particular to buy, though, and it's the last place in town where you run into people by accident rather than by arrangement. That isn't a small thing, and it exists precisely because the place is too full. So I've made my peace with it, and I do the real shopping at half past eight.

what_lifts_it.point: A participle clause and an imperative conditional replace band 7's standard if-clauses.
'Heaving', 'swallows an hour', 'faintly disloyal' sit exactly where a native would put them.
It ends on a settled position and the behaviour that follows from it.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to tell about a place where I was going when I was a child. It was an old railway near the house of my grandparents. The train was not there any more, so it is only trees and bushes, and there was a hole in the fence, so we can go inside.

I went there with my brother and two boys from our street. We go there every day in the summer holiday, when I was seven, eight, until maybe twelve years old.

We did many things there. We took some wood from a building place and we make a house, but always it is falling down and we build it again. In August we eat the blackberries. Also we put coins on the rail because we wanted to make them flat.

I remember it very well because it was our place, only for children. No adults came there. So we can do everything we want. Now it is a bicycle road with a bench, and my nephew goes there, but he doesn't know about our house. It is a little bit sad, but it is normal. This is the place from my childhood.

Every stage of the story arrives in the same flat two-clause sentence.
'Many things', 'very well', 'a little bit sad' — the wording never gets more exact.

model_answers.label: The target — same memory, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place I'd talk about is an old railway embankment at the end of the street where my grandparents lived. The line had closed long before I was born, so by the time we found it, it was completely wild — brambles, birch trees, and a fence with a gap in it that everybody's parents pretended not to know about.

I went up there with my brother and two boys from the next street, more or less every day of the summer holidays, from when I was about seven until I was twelve or thirteen and it suddenly stopped being interesting.

What we did there was mostly build things. We dragged pallets up from behind the builders' yard and made a den against the bank, which collapsed regularly and got rebuilt slightly better each time. We picked blackberries in August, and we spent an unreasonable amount of time trying to flatten coins on the one length of rail that was still there. None of it was allowed, strictly speaking, and none of it was ever stopped.

As for why it's stayed with me so clearly — I think it's because it was the first place that was properly ours. Nobody had planned it for us and no adult ever came up there, so whatever happened was entirely our own doing. It's a cycle path now, tarmacked and signposted, with a bench roughly where the den was. My nephew rides along it and has no idea. I'm glad it's used, but there's nothing about it now that a child could claim.

what_lifts_it.point: Two past perfects and a passive hold the timeline that band 6 kept losing.
'Pretended not to know about', 'an unreasonable amount of time' — chunks with attitude in them.
The turn ends in the present day, which closes the story instead of stopping it.

annotations.why: Negative past clauses handled cleanly are strong grammar evidence.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The place was a disused railway embankment at the end of my grandparents' road. The line had been lifted decades earlier, so what remained was a long green corridor running behind the houses, reached through a gap in the fence that every parent on that street knew about and none of them ever mentioned.

I was up there with my brother and a couple of boys from the next street on most days of the summer, from about seven until the year I turned thirteen and abruptly stopped going.

Chiefly, we built. Pallets were hauled up from the builders' yard behind the church, a den went against the bank, it fell down within a fortnight, and we rebuilt it marginally better each time. There were blackberries in August, and an absurd amount of effort spent flattening coins on the last surviving stretch of rail. None of that was permitted and none of it was ever prevented.

Why it has stayed with me is straightforward enough: it was the first territory that belonged to us. Nothing about it had been provided, which is precisely what made it valuable — no adult had ever set foot up there, so everything that happened was our own work and our own fault. It's a cycle path now, resurfaced and signposted, with a bench roughly where the den stood. My nephew uses it and hasn't the faintest idea. I'm pleased it's in use. I just doubt any child will ever call it theirs.

'Lifted', 'hauled', 'territory', 'resurfaced' are precise rather than decorative.
It concedes the modern use and then refuses it, in two short sentences.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a town in the mountains where I went last year in November. It is about three hours by car from my parents house.

Before I go, I think it will be very beautiful. I saw many photos on internet, with sun and colourful houses and people sitting outside. So I expected the same thing.

But when I arrived, there was fog everywhere. For two days I cannot see the mountains, and the mountains are the reason to go there. Also two cafés were closed for the winter, and the museum was closed too. I was very disappointed and I thought it is a waste of money.

But after, it became better. Because everything was closed, all the people were in the same café, and I talked with an old lady for all the afternoon. She lived there all her life and she told me many things about the tourists in the town. It was very interesting, more interesting than the photos. So in the end I was happy, but also a little bit strange feeling, because I wanted a place like the photos. This is my experience.

what_caps_it.point: Nothing is backshifted: 'I think it will be' and 'I thought it is' inside one past story.
The reversal is flagged with 'but after' and then never developed into a point.
'Very beautiful', 'very disappointed', 'very interesting' stand in for any precision.

annotations.label: Cause before result
annotations.why: Keep this — a 'because' clause at the front organises the whole sentence.

annotations.label: The whole sentence is present

annotations.label: Present modal in a past story
annotations.why: 'I couldn't see the mountains.' Past story, past modal.

annotations.span: I thought it is a waste of money
annotations.label: No backshift after 'thought'
annotations.why: 'I thought it was a waste of money.' The reported clause moves back too.

annotations.label: An article that shouldn't be there
annotations.why: 'All afternoon' or 'the whole afternoon' — you cannot have both.

model_answers.label: The target — same trip, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place was a small town in the mountains, about three hours' drive from where my family live, and I went there for a long weekend in November.

What I'd expected was essentially the photographs. Every image I'd seen of it was taken in September — clear light, painted houses, people eating outside — so I'd built up quite a specific picture of wandering around in the sun and taking a great many photographs of my own.

What I actually got was fog. The whole valley was under cloud for two days and you couldn't see the mountains at all, which are the only reason anyone goes. Two of the three cafés had shut for the winter, the museum was closed for repairs, and the one bus up to the ridge wasn't running either. By the second morning I'd more or less decided the trip was a write-off.

And then it wasn't, oddly. Because everything else was shut, everyone still in the town ended up in the same café, and I spent an entire afternoon talking to a woman in her eighties who had lived there her whole life and had a great deal to say about what the visitors had done to the place. I learned far more from that than I would have from a clear day, and she wasn't remotely sentimental about any of it. So what I came away with was a slightly uncomfortable feeling — that the version of the town I'd wanted was the version that had been produced for me.

what_lifts_it.point: Four past perfects hold the expectation apart from the reality throughout.
'A write-off', 'built up a picture', 'a great deal to say' — chunks instead of intensifiers.
Two clearly marked turns, and the answer ends on a judgement about itself.

annotations.label: Answers bullet two in one line
annotations.why: State the expectation as a thing, then spend your time on the evidence.

annotations.span: Every image I'd seen of it was taken in September
annotations.label: Past perfect inside a past clause
annotations.why: Backshift once and both layers of time stay obvious to the listener.

annotations.span: the trip was a write-off
annotations.label: One noun makes the judgement
annotations.why: Reuse 'a write-off' for any plan or day that came to nothing.

annotations.span: What I actually got was fog.
annotations.label: A short sentence marks the turn
annotations.why: Five words after a long sentence signal the reversal without a linker.

annotations.span: And then it wasn't, oddly.
annotations.label: A second, deliberate reversal
annotations.why: Two turns keep a listener with you far better than one does.

annotations.span: I learned far more from that than I would have from a clear day
annotations.label: Comparative against a hypothetical
annotations.why: Comparing what happened with what didn't earns real grammar credit.

annotations.span: had a great deal to say about what the visitors had done to the place
annotations.label: Reports an opinion without quoting
annotations.why: Summarising what somebody said avoids a long run of direct speech.

annotations.span: the version of the town I'd wanted was the version that had been produced for me
annotations.label: Contrastive stress on 'produced'
annotations.why: The entire point sits on one word, so give that word the beat.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This was a small mountain town three hours from my parents', and I went up for a long weekend at the end of November, which was my first mistake.

Everything I'd seen of the place had been photographed in September, mostly by people who had gone at the right time of year. Clear light, painted shutters, people eating outside — so that was the weekend I'd packed for and, in effect, paid for.

What I found was cloud. The valley stayed under it for two solid days, so the mountains, which are the entire point, might as well not have existed. Two of the three cafés had closed for the season, the museum was mid-refurbishment, and the bus up to the ridge had stopped running in October. By Saturday lunchtime I'd written the trip off completely.

Which is when it got interesting. With nothing else open, everybody still in the town converged on the one café that was, and I spent most of an afternoon with a woman in her eighties who'd been born in the next street and had a good deal to say — not much of it warm — about what tourism had done to the valley and to the people who had stayed in it. I came away having learned more than any amount of scenery would have taught me, and faintly uneasy with myself, because what I'd gone looking for was the version of that town that had been arranged for people like me.

what_lifts_it.point: 'Might as well not have existed' and a cleft with a past perfect passive go past band 7.
'Converged', 'mid-refurbishment', 'not much of it warm' are dry and exact, never showy.
The self-criticism at the end is the point of the turn and it is made only once.

annotations.span: which was my first mistake
annotations.label: An aside that flags the structure
annotations.why: Signalling trouble early makes a listener wait for the payoff.

annotations.span: might as well not have existed
annotations.label: Modal perfect in a relative clause
annotations.why: A compact way of saying the whole thing failed, and it sounds spoken.

annotations.span: Which is when it got interesting.
annotations.label: Turns the story in five words
annotations.why: A short fragment after a long paragraph is the cleanest reversal available.

annotations.span: not much of it warm
annotations.label: Four words replace a sentence
annotations.why: An aside like this shows judgement without any adjective of your own.

annotations.span: what I'd gone looking for was the version of that town that had been arranged for people like me
annotations.label: Cleft plus past perfect passive
annotations.why: Front the 'what' clause so the turn ends on the phrase that matters.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I would like to talk about a change in my town. I want that they close the main street for the cars, near the market, maybe two hundred metres.

The reason is because the market is dying. Everybody says it is the supermarkets, but I think it is the traffic. There are always cars between the stalls and the shops, so it is dangerous and it is very loud. Old people cannot cross the road, and people with a baby cannot cross also. And in front there is a big shop which is closed since three years.

For do this, the council must do it, because the street is theirs. Also the bus company, because the buses go there. And the shop owners, but they don't want it, they think if there is no cars, nobody comes to their shops.

If they close the street, it will be much better. There is more space for the market. And people will stay more time, because now everybody walks fast and goes home. When people stay, they meet other people. So this is my change and I hope one day they do it.

what_caps_it.point: The whole answer is imagined, yet every conditional in it is built as though it were real.
Reasons arrive as short clauses stitched together with 'and' and 'also'.
'Better', 'dangerous', 'loud' — nothing here would survive into a Part 3 answer.

annotations.span: Everybody says it is the supermarkets, but I think it is the traffic.
annotations.label: Rejects the obvious cause
annotations.why: Keep this — disagreeing with the easy explanation is a genuine band-7 habit.

annotations.span: I want that they close the main street
annotations.label: 'Want' cannot take that
annotations.why: 'I'd like them to close the main street.' Want takes object plus 'to'.

annotations.span: The reason is because
annotations.label: Two connectors, one job
annotations.why: 'The reason is that…' or simply 'because…', but never both at once.

annotations.span: which is closed since three years
annotations.label: Wrong tense with 'since'
annotations.why: 'Which has been closed for three years.' Duration needs a perfect form.

annotations.span: For do this
annotations.label: Preposition before a bare verb
annotations.why: 'To do this.' Purpose takes an infinitive, never 'for' plus verb.

annotations.span: If they close the street, it will be much better.
annotations.label: Real conditional for an imagined change
annotations.why: 'If they closed it, it would be much better.' The card is hypothetical.

model_answers.label: The target — same proposal, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The change I'd like is fairly small in scale — I'd close about two hundred metres of the main street to cars, the stretch that runs past the market, and move the buses one street over.

The reason is that the market is slowly dying, and I don't think it's dying for the obvious reason. It isn't the supermarket, or not only. It's that there's a constant line of traffic between the stalls and the pavement, so you can't cross, you can't hear, and nobody with a pushchair or a walking frame will attempt it. The department store opposite has been boarded up for three years, and every time a shop shuts it takes a bit more footfall with it.

Making it happen would need three parties who don't currently agree on anything. The council, who own the road, the bus company, who would have to accept a longer route, and the traders themselves, who are convinced that taking the cars out would finish them off. I understand why they think that, and I'd probably think it too if my rent depended on it, but the evidence from the next town along suggests the opposite.

So what difference would it make? Practically, you'd more or less double the usable space in front of the stalls, which the traders could take over. But the real change would be that people would linger. Nobody stands still on that street at the moment, and a town where nobody stands still is a town where nothing accidental happens. You buy what you came for and you leave.

what_lifts_it.point: Second conditionals and 'would have to' are handled consistently across the whole turn.
'Footfall', 'finish them off', 'linger' — the words belong to the subject, not to a list.
Each bullet gets a signposted paragraph and the last one ranks two arguments.

annotations.label: States the change and its size
annotations.why: Naming the scale early stops the proposal sounding like a daydream.

annotations.span: I don't think it's dying for the obvious reason
annotations.label: Refuses the easy explanation
annotations.why: Rejecting the obvious cause obliges you to supply a better one.

annotations.span: you can't cross, you can't hear, and nobody with a pushchair or a walking frame will attempt it
annotations.label: Three parallel clauses
annotations.why: Parallel structure is grammar you can plan for in advance.

annotations.span: it takes a bit more footfall with it
annotations.label: The trade word, used naturally
annotations.why: One precise term proves you know the subject, not just the vocabulary.

annotations.span: who would have to accept a longer route
annotations.label: 'Would have to' for imagined duty
annotations.why: This is the workhorse structure for any change you are proposing.

annotations.span: So what difference would it make?
annotations.label: Asks the bullet as a question
annotations.why: Turning the bullet into a question is the cleanest signpost there is.

annotations.span: the real change would be that people would linger
annotations.label: One verb carries the argument
annotations.why: 'Linger' means stop, stay and look, without three separate verbs.

annotations.span: You buy what you came for and you leave.
annotations.label: Deliberately flat ending
annotations.why: Let the last clause drop away; the flatness is itself the point.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The change I'd argue for is a modest one: closing a couple of hundred metres of the main street to traffic, the stretch alongside the market, and diverting the buses onto the road behind it.

The market is dying, and the usual explanation, which is the supermarket out on the bypass, strikes me as only half true. The other half is that there's a permanent queue of cars between the stalls and the shopfronts, so the street is impossible to cross, impossible to hear across, and quietly hostile to anybody slow. With the department store opposite boarded up since 2022, each closure drags a little more footfall out with it.

Getting it off the ground would need three parties who agree on very little: the council, who own the road; the bus company, who'd be asked to swallow a longer route; and the traders, who are convinced that removing the cars would ruin them. Their fear is perfectly rational, and I'd share it if my rent depended on that street. It just happens to be contradicted by every comparable town I know of.

The obvious gain is space, and quite a lot of it. The less obvious one, and I think the important one, is that people would stop moving. Nobody stands still on that street at present, and a town in which nobody stands still is a town where nothing unplanned ever happens. You buy what you came for and you go home.

what_lifts_it.point: A 'with' participle clause and a hedged passive replace band 7's plain relative clauses.
'Quietly hostile', 'swallow a longer route', 'drags footfall out' are exact and unshowy.
It grants the objectors' logic before rejecting their conclusion, which band 7 only implies.

annotations.span: quietly hostile to anybody slow
annotations.label: Four words instead of a sentence
annotations.why: Give the street an attitude and the argument largely makes itself.

annotations.span: With the department store opposite boarded up since 2022
annotations.label: 'With' plus a participle clause
annotations.why: A compact way to add background without building another sentence.

annotations.span: who'd be asked to swallow a longer route
annotations.label: 'Swallow' carries the reluctance
annotations.why: Choose a verb that shows how a party feels about what they're given.

annotations.span: It just happens to be contradicted by every comparable town I know of.
annotations.label: Hedged passive after a concession
annotations.why: Grant the reasoning, then disagree with the conclusion, in one clause.

annotations.span: The less obvious one, and I think the important one, is that people would stop moving.
annotations.label: Ranks two arguments aloud
annotations.why: Saying which of your points matters more is exactly what gets rewarded.

I want to describe something in my house that I must replace. It is our sofa, it is green and it has three places for sitting.

We have it since nine years. I bought it from my colleague, she was going to another country, and it was very cheap, only eighty pounds. So it was a good price for us.

Now there are many problems. The cushion in the left side is broken, so when you sit there you are lower than the other people. Also there is a spring inside and you can feel it in your back. The colour is not same in all the parts, because of the sun from the window. And our cat, he scratches the corner every day.

Why I don't buy a new one? First, because sofas are expensive. But also there is another problem: our door is very small, and I think a new sofa cannot pass. The old sofa came before we changed the door. So every time I look for a sofa, I remember this and I stop. Maybe we will keep it forever.

annotations.why: Choose one of them: 'our cat scratches the corner'.

model_answers.label: The target — same sofa, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The thing I'd talk about is our sofa, which is a three-seater, dark green, and quite obviously on its last legs.

We've had it about nine years. I bought it second-hand from a colleague who was moving abroad, for something like eighty pounds, which felt like a bargain at the time and has worked out at under a tenner a year. It's the only thing in that flat which has genuinely paid for itself.

What's wrong with it is fairly comprehensive. The cushion on the left has collapsed, so anybody sitting there sinks about six inches lower than everyone else. One of the springs has worked its way loose and you can feel it through the fabric if you lean back properly. The arms have faded by completely different amounts, depending on how close they are to the window. And the cat has done to one corner exactly what cats do. None of that is anybody's fault, mind you; it's nine years of ordinary use.

So why is it still there? Partly money, obviously — sofas cost more than I want to spend on somewhere to sit. But mostly it's that I measured the door frame about a year ago and discovered that almost nothing sold now would actually fit through it — this sofa came in before we had the front door replaced. So replacing it isn't really a sofa problem, it's a door problem, and every time I get as far as looking at sofas I remember that and give up. I suspect it'll outlast us both.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect for duration and 'one of the springs has' are both handled correctly.
'On its last legs', 'worked its way loose', 'under a tenner a year' — chunks with content.
The last bullet reframes the problem instead of restating the price.

annotations.span: quite obviously on its last legs
annotations.label: Idiom used at the right moment
annotations.why: 'On its last legs' fits any object, machine or plan that is failing.

annotations.span: We've had it about nine years.
annotations.label: Present perfect for duration
annotations.why: Possession that still holds takes 'have had', never the past simple.

annotations.span: has worked out at under a tenner a year
annotations.label: Arithmetic as evaluation
annotations.why: Working the cost out per year persuades far better than 'it was cheap'.

annotations.span: What's wrong with it is fairly comprehensive.
annotations.label: Heads the bullet, dryly
annotations.why: One summary sentence buys you four examples with no hesitation.

annotations.span: One of the springs has worked its way loose
annotations.label: Singular verb after 'one of the'
annotations.why: The verb belongs to 'one', never to the plural noun beside it.

annotations.span: So why is it still there?
annotations.label: Turns the bullet into a question
annotations.why: Ask the bullet aloud and you cannot then forget to answer it.

annotations.span: replacing it isn't really a sofa problem, it's a door problem
annotations.label: Reframes the whole answer
annotations.why: Naming the real obstacle is what lifts an ordinary object card.

annotations.span: I suspect it'll outlast us both.
annotations.label: Quiet drop on the last line
annotations.why: A soft ending sounds finished; a loud one sounds like you ran out.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The obvious candidate is our sofa: three seats, dark green, and visibly finished.

We've had it nine years. I bought it off a colleague who was emigrating, for eighty pounds, which struck me as a bargain then and has since worked out at rather less than a tenner a year — the only purchase in that flat I can honestly say that about. Whether that reflects well on the sofa or badly on everything else, I couldn't tell you.

Its faults are extensive. The left-hand cushion gave up years ago, so whoever sits there ends up several inches below the rest of the room. A spring has escaped somewhere behind the fabric and makes itself known if you lean back. The arms have faded at conspicuously different rates according to their distance from the window. And the cat has done to one corner precisely what cats do. None of it is anyone's fault; it is nine years of ordinary use.

The interesting question is why it's still in the room, and the answer isn't really money. About a year ago I measured the door frame and worked out that virtually nothing on sale now would come through it; the sofa predates the front door we had fitted. So this isn't a sofa problem at all, it's a door problem, which is a considerably more expensive thing to admit. Every time I get as far as browsing I remember that and stop. Realistically, the sofa will see me out.

what_lifts_it.point: A 'whoever' clause and a sentential 'which' go past band 7's ordinary relatives.
'Predates', 'conspicuously', 'see me out' are dry and exact rather than decorative.
The reframing arrives as the punchline of the turn instead of as an explanation.

annotations.span: whoever sits there ends up several inches below the rest of the room
annotations.label: 'Whoever' as a subject clause
annotations.why: A cleaner way to generalise than 'if a person sits there'.

annotations.span: faded at conspicuously different rates
annotations.label: Precision where band 6 said colour
annotations.why: Describe the process rather than the state and the picture sharpens.

annotations.span: the sofa predates the front door we had fitted
annotations.label: One verb replaces a clause
annotations.why: 'Predates' carries 'came before' in a single word and fits the register.

annotations.span: which is a considerably more expensive thing to admit
annotations.label: Relative clause on a whole idea
annotations.why: 'Which' can refer to your entire previous sentence, not just to a noun.

annotations.span: Realistically, the sofa will see me out.
annotations.label: A one-line landing
annotations.why: Finish on a short dry sentence and the whole turn sounds complete.

question_notes.answer_shape: Answer the conditional, name the group who wouldn't, then explain why not.
question_notes.watch_out: Keep 'would' throughout and don't drift into what happens today.

question_notes.answer_shape: Take a direction, name the group driving it, then hedge the prediction.

teaching.band_move: Answer with what people do and what it costs them. Waste questions go vague when they stay moral.
